items.title: I Built My Own AI Agent Orchestration Tool
items.story_key: story|title:i built my own ai agent orchestration tool
items.content_excerpt: I run a lot of AI coding agents, often around 10 at the same time, and easily 20 if I count subagents. With the tools I had, that meant I forgot about the ones that mattered and never knew when one needed me, so I polled all of them, all day. Coming back to a parked project was draining, because the context was gone. So I built my own AI agent orchestration tool: a map. It's called Agentic Crafting Table (ACT), it's open source, and a few of my colleagues at Checkly use it now too. Since I started working this way, I merge up to twice as many PRs a week as I did in the six months before, and it doesn't feel like juggling. If you want to build your own tooling, I hope this post inspires you and saves you some time. A terminal multiplexer with one pane per agent works for two agents and stops working at six: every pane looks the same, and answering "is this one waiting on me?" means reading a lot of text. A chat app per task is nicer to look at, but it has the same problem, and the ticket, the Slack thread and the RFC are still in other windows or buried in the conversation. I really liked how freeform whiteboard and diagramming apps are, but they had no live view of my agents. Most of them made me read a wall of text to get context, and none of them kept the relevant information close to the work. Most AI tooling still lives at the level of the artifact: the editor, the agent, its output. I didn't need another layer on top of tools that already work, like GitHub for code reviews and Linear for tickets. I wanted something around them. What I wanted was a layer on top of what I actually do all day: collect supporting information and evidence, manage agents that write code, review code, roll it out and validate it. And I needed the context around all of that to stay easy to reach. Agentic Crafting Table (ACT) is an open source desktop app that puts all your work on one zoomable map. Every project is its own neighbourhood, and every piece of work is an item on the map: an agent session, a ticket, a note, a PR, a review, a rollout. You link items to show what feeds what. Agents are plain Claude Code or Codex sessions, started in the project folder. ACT gives them an MCP server, so they can read the map and put their own things on it. And because the session runs inside ACT, the app knows when an agent stops or asks a question. items.title: NOX Local – a coding agent for 4B models on an 8 GB GPU
items.story_key: story|ver:4|title:nox local a coding agent for 4b models on an 8 gb gpu
items.content_excerpt: Terminal coding agent for local models: own TUI, llama.cpp on an 8 GB GPU, MCP, skills, plan mode. Offline and free. NØX-Local is a coding agent for people who want the work to stay on their own computer. It drives llama.cpp directly, so there is no API key, no account, no per-token bill and nothing sent to a server. The whole agent loop is built around one constraint most agents ignore: a 4B model has to be able to use it. Cloud agents stop when your quota runs out, and they see every file they read. A local model is free and private, but the agent loops written for frontier models fall apart on it: too many tools, prompts that fill the window, and tool calls the small model formats slightly wrong. The numbers on the reference machine (RX 6500 XT 8 GB, Ryzen 5 5600GT, 16 GB DDR4) are in docs/BENCHMARKS.md . No GPU? llama-server falls back to the CPU and NØX-Local runs, but expect a few tokens per second. The smallest model is the one to try. NØX-Local looks for llama-server in $NOX_LLAMA_SERVER , then PATH , then ~/.nox-local/llama.cpp , then ~/.nox/llama.cpp . If your build is somewhere else, set the variable: Models are stored as plain GGUF files in ~/models (change it with NOX_MODELS ). Any llama.cpp-compatible GGUF works; the catalog only lists the ones measured here. Type a request. In auto mode the agent edits files and runs commands, and asks before anything risky. Shift+Tab cycles the mode, Ctrl+O picks another model, Ctrl+C twice quits. The answer should mention real files, and the output should include a tool call. If it answers from memory instead, the model is too small for tools — try the 9B. Five models, measured on the reference machine: AMD Radeon RX 6500 XT 8 GB (Vulkan, RADV), Ryzen 5 5600GT, 16 GB DDR4, running Omarchy 4.5 (Arch Linux). Settings are the ones NØX-Local uses: --fit placement, KV cache q8_0, flash attention. All five run on an 8 GB card. Pick with /model ; the conversation carries over and the model reloads on your next message. -m <id> starts on a specific one. The numbers come from llama-bench ( -p 512 -n 128 , q8_0 KV, flash attention) on that machine, except Saluki, which does not fit on the GPU alone and was measured through llama-server --fit . Other GPUs work; expect different numbers. Method and older measurements: docs/BENCHMARKS.md . Keys worth knowing: Shift+Tab mode, Ctrl+T effort, Ctrl+O model, Esc interrupt, Alt+Enter queue a message for the running turn, Ctrl+K palette. Every change that is not a plain read

items.title: Not Every Agent Hibernates
items.story_key: story|title:not every agent hibernates
items.content_excerpt: Distinguished Engineer for AI at VMware Cloud Foundation. Writing about AI infrastructure, GPU platform design, and NUMA-aware architecture. Hibernation is often presented as the answer to running agents at scale: suspend the idle ones, keep their state, and bring them back when there is work. It sounds like a fleet-wide feature. It is not. Of the four common agent patterns, only two ever suspend. The other two are either removed when their work is done or never stop running until it is. The previous article ended at the platform layer: how fast a sandbox starts or resumes shapes the wait between model calls, and that is the layer a platform team controls. Before that speed can be tuned, it has to be clear when a sandbox starts, suspends, and resumes at all, and whether an agent has one. The previous articles in this series followed a single agent run from the inside: what an agent is and when it is worth building , which components run the agent loop , what reaches the inference endpoint , and why the agent resends its context with every call . This article zooms out to the session: which agents need a sandbox, where sandbox start, suspend, and resume fall in the session lifecycle, and which waits give the platform a chance to suspend an agent at all. The agent loop is covered in Anatomy of an Agentic Workload : a trigger starts the harness, the harness calls the model endpoint, executes the tool calls the model returns, adds the results to the context, and repeats until the model gives a final answer. Tools that run code execute in a sandbox. Not every agent needs one: an agent whose tools only call remote APIs, such as a mail or calendar agent, runs without a sandbox, and its harness sends tool calls directly to those APIs. That article follows one run. Agents rarely stop after one. This article adds the terms needed to describe what happens across runs: The harnesses and sandboxes run on what this article calls the agent cluster. The model endpoints run separately, on a model cluster or at a model provider, with their own lifecycle. Agents range from bounded requests to extended tasks and recurring responsibilities. They differ most in how long they run and what state must persist once their work stops. A short-lived agent handles a bounded task, one with a defined end that finishes in seconds to minutes. items.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Linguistic Annotation
items.summary: Assessing large language models for linguistic annotation requires task-specific evaluation under documented conditions. We present dhAIBench, a Python benchmarking and annotation tool with a web interface for exploring and sharing results. It records prompts, configurations and predictions, enabling comparisons of annotation quality, confidence calibration, repeatability and estimated cost. We demonstrate the framework and the associated methodology through 293 runs of 48 models on nine linguistic annotation tasks spanning morphology, syntax, semantics, discourse-pragmatics, spelling normalization and learner-language correction. Models achieve high agreement with reference annotations on several tasks, including those on non-standardized, historical varieties as well as requiring contextual interpretation. The results support evaluating models against specific linguistic tasks, rather than relying on general rankings. To this end, we make the current and future benchmarks publicly available at dhaibench.silent3.ff.cuni.cz.

items.title: Detection-Efficient Watermarking for Vision--Language Agents via Risk-Constrained Strength Allocation
items.summary: Vision--language agents generate descriptions, decisions, and instructions that may be reused by users, downstream agents, and automated workflows, creating a need for provenance mechanisms that support content authenticity and post-deployment auditing without unnecessarily degrading response quality. We present a risk-aware semantic watermarking framework that combines predictive uncertainty with a zero-shot multimodal relevance-risk proxy to allocate watermark strength during decoding. A single risk penalty $λ$ exposes a continuous operating frontier, allowing deployment-time selection of a detection--quality trade-off without model retraining. At a selected operating point, mean watermark strength is reduced by approximately 59.4\% relative to fixed-strength watermarking, while perplexity change falls from 0.3634 to 0.1689 and clean/paraphrased ROC-AUC reaches 0.9552/0.9459. A matched-strength analysis shows that this advantage reflects the allocation policy rather than lower average intervention: at comparable mean strength, risk-constrained allocation achieves substantially higher ROC-AUC than fixed, entropy-only, and criticality-only policies, identifying it as detection-efficient rather than quality-dominant. We further show that threshold calibration on finite samples produces substantial false-positive-rate drift, motivating calibration variance reporting as standard practice for auditable provenance.

items.title: ScenarioForge: Resource-Grounded Generation and Execution Validation of Cyber Exercises
items.summary: Cyber-range and capture-the-flag scenario construction remains labor-intensive because authors must coordinate infrastructure, vulnerable services, attack paths, artifacts, and success conditions. LLMs can propose detailed exercises, but plausible descriptions do not guarantee deployable software or verifiable objectives. We present ScenarioForge, which turns high-level requirements into resource-grounded topologies, services, traffic, segmentation, and challenge chains, then instantiates and validates them in the Common Open Research Emulator (CORE). The ScenarioForge Execution Dataset contains 226 materialized scenarios covering 294 Vulhub images and all 85 custom-built challenge-resource generators developed with our AI-assisted scaffolding. All 226 passed construction, preview, sequencing, deployment, strict runtime validation, and live artifact checks; their 867 steps, each an individually verifiable challenge objective, comprise 457 vulnerability-backed and 410 generated-resource-backed instances. In a separate 50-prompt matched benchmark, ScenarioForge+Qwen3.8 and ScenarioForge+GPT5.6 each achieved 50/50 (100%) topology/build success and 160/160 intent fields; direct frontier generation reached 41/50 builds and 147/160 fields only with the full cumulative scaffold: structure, vocabulary, policy, and container-image guidance. The test still omitted ScenarioForge's downstream challenge-resource generation, dependency/flag sequencing, deployment, and live validation. The artifacts support operationally rich, reproducible exercises for training and evaluation.

items.title: Harness Leverage Across Model Size: A Ladder of Five Local Agent Harnesses from 0.75B to 4.7B
items.summary: A harness turns a model into a system that completes tasks: it builds the prompt, exposes tools and decides when work is done. Harness comparisons hold the model fixed. Model comparisons hold the harness fixed. We vary both: five shipped harnesses, 18 artifact-producing tasks, four locally deployable open-weight models from 0.75B to 4.7B and a 35.5B anchor, with one deterministic checker scoring all 360 ladder cells. The completion-controlling harness, Mingbird, has the highest mean at every size. Of four pre-registered paired contrasts, two survive Holm correction, at 0.75B and 4.7B. Thirteen of sixteen paired intervals exclude zero under the deployment reading, with leads from 0.075 over the strongest rival to 0.819 over the weakest. The completion gate is not the carrier: disabling all six executable checks moves the mean by +0.080, +0.117, +0.003 and -0.004, every interval including zero, and only at 1.9B does disabling it create empty runs. Removing one repeat-blocking rule alone costs 0.411 at 0.75B and leaves eight of eighteen tasks with no artifact. The harness effect is a progress effect: it decides whether a run leaves anything on disk. Of 357 usable cells, 127 leave none of their declared artifacts and 85 of those exit normally, so a scorer that reads exit status credits work that was never written. Whether the effect grows or shrinks with size, four rungs cannot settle: a floor arm produces a rise, a ceiling a decline, and a cross-family rung a peak.

items.content_excerpt: TL;DR: On one NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, vLLM serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 1.7M tokens/s per GPU while each user gets 387 tokens/s, 58× GB300 NVL72, and reaches 2.52M at peak throughput and 1,810 tokens/s for a single user. The gains come from building on what is new in Rubin: kernels tuned for its split memory and FP4 tensor cores, specialized decode kernels for low latency, and a rack-wide KV cache and Engram tables shared over NVLink. This is the third post in our DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash series. The first post covered day-0 bring-up and kernel fusions. The second scaled the model to a GB300 NVL72 rack with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP. This post moves the same stack to Vera Rubin NVL72, which we introduced last month . Rubin opens up new avenues for optimization. We start with the hardware facts that shaped our work, then go through four groups of optimizations: Figure 1: SemiAnalysis AgentX on NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 (vLLM, P/D disaggregation, Wide-EP) vs. GB300 NVL72. Throughput counts cached input, uncached input and output tokens ( GB300 source ). We measure performance with the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark as a representative agentic serving workload, aligned with our previous posts. Figure 1 compares the two racks' raw throughput (total tokens per GPU per second, including input, cached, and output) and power-normalized throughput, respectively in two tabs. We use the same methodology as in our previous GB300 post . For kernels and model forward profiling, vllm bench forward times exact prefill and decode batches through the real execute_model path, with real weights and real AgentX tokens. We A/B prefill kernels in loops that run for several seconds and report sustained numbers where they differ. Three properties of Vera Rubin NVL72 drove most of the decisions below. Where an optimization is specific to Rubin, we say which of them it relies on. Figure 2: Weight stages of the routed-expert GEMM in one SM's shared memory, with the SM100 MXFP8×MXFP4 MMA and with SM107's K64 MXFP8×MXFP4 MMA on packed FP4. We kept GB300's three engine shapes: DEP2 prefill, Wide-EP decode (DEP16 or DEP32), and a TP decode path for the lowest latency (next section). We also kept DeepSeek's kernel set (MegaMoE, MegaAttn, Mega-mHC, MegaGate, DeepSelect) and rebuilt much of it for SM107. At 32K tokens per rank, a prefill step is dominated by the expert GEMMs; most of the rest goes into streaming the residual and attention's working set through HBM. So this round went in

items.title: Goal Engineering
items.summary: The future of agents is them taking on open ended goals and driving towards completion of those goals. Learn more.
items.story_key: story|title:goal engineering
items.content_excerpt: The scope of tasks that agents can take on has increased drastically over the past few years. They have gone from simple text generation to tool calling and decision making to executing full tasks. The future of agents is them taking on open ended goals and driving towards completion of those goals. Launches like that of Hone give us a glimpse into that future. In this world, designing the scope of agents is crucial. Point them in the wrong direction, and you’ll get a lot of wasted tokens. A key part of the Hone agent set up is defining metrics for them to optimize. As we’ve worked on similar styles of agents, we’ve realized something about designing the scope for agents: you want to design the scope of an agent such that it makes it as easy as possible to give feedback as the agent operates within that scope. When agents mess up, a big reason they mess up is lack of right context. In order to fix this, you need to give the agent the right context. There are different types of context. Some types of context are things like access to the right documents or APIs - that is relatively easy to fix. The trickiest context to give the agent is context that is not written down anywhere already. This context needs to be given to the agent as feedback from a human expert. This is especially important as agents expand beyond doing verifiable tasks and start taking on subjective work alongside humans within an organization. For example, if you want an agent to help optimize a business metric (like improving your ads to optimize marketing performance), there are so many nuances beyond just factual context that you want to govern how the agent behaves. You probably have a certain taste around what sounds and looks good. You have opinions about how provocative or out-there your brand can be. An agent that can’t effectively get feedback to learn these things quickly becomes useless. If the scope of your agent makes it really easy to give lots of high quality feedback on the agent’s work, that will help you immensely in building an agent that can reliably pursue a long-horizon goal. A related learning is that you want to invest a lot in an intuitive and delightful UX for reviewing agent work. The bottleneck for agents performing is often them learning from feedback. Therefore, you should seek to optimize ease and quality of feedback collection! Investing in a clear UX for that is a worthwhile investment. items.title: claude-code v2.1.323
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added Code Mode, an experimental opt-in in which Claude writes JavaScript to call its tools; see https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-mode to turn it on, or to turn it off for an organization
  • Added engines["claude-code"] to plugin.json: plugins outside their stated Claude Code version range are not installed, updated or loaded, and install and update pick the newest version that fits
  • Added type checking of a plugin's TypeScript hooks module to claude plugin validate; each finding is a warning, and --strict fails on it
  • Added to claude plugin validate the $ nouns a mod's engine.create hook adds, withholds or replaces
  • Added support for CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_MODEL in managed settings for Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers (takes effect once Claude Desktop includes this version)
  • Added an options menu (stop, switch to usage credits, upgrade) when a model needs usage credits that are turned off or used up
  • Added a progress heartbeat every 30 seconds while hooks run long in claude -p and SDK sessions, so a host such as Claude Desktop won't end the turn as hung (once it includes this version)
  • Added .docx support to Artifact tool asset uploads
  • Added a /diff to close hint to the diff panel, and the keys that focus and close a panel to the ? shortcut guide
  • Added a start-up warning for Bash allow rules with a * in a variable's value, such as Bash(PORT=* npm run dev)
  • Added a warning when a plugin's language server can't start, naming the server and what to check
  • Added a one-time startup notice naming CLAUDE_CODE_PERFORCE_MODE when Perforce settings are found and the mode is off

  • Added unsetOptionCount to the claude plugin install --json result: how many userConfig options are not yet set
  • Added isPromptCovered to the props a mod's pane is drawn with, telling it when a dialog or a field above the prompt covers the prompt

  • Fixed a resumed session joining your next message to an old interrupted message that was not resumed
  • Fixed a memory spike at the next prompt after Claude changed a very large file
  • Fixed a setting saved in a running session undoing a hand edit made to settings.json moments earlier; a settings file you delete during a session now stays deleted
  • Fixed claude plugin commands and claude mcp list signing you out of a Console profile when they ended while the token was being renewed

items.title: Kitesurf is now open source
items.summary: Kitesurf, our experimental browser engine for AI agents, is now open source. Inspect the code, run it locally, or deploy your own instance on Cloudflare Workers.
items.story_key: story|title:kitesurf is now open source
items.content_excerpt: We introduced Kitesurf , our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to. That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers. Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer. Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network. Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation. Kitesurf builds on Cloudflare’s Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly: These projects made Kitesurf possible. They retain their respective licenses; the repository's NOTICE documents third-party notices. Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result. All packages, the engine, its Rust core, DOM shims, renderer, and Kitesurf CLI live separately in folders under the repository’s packages directory where you can explore how all the pieces fit together. To run Kitesurf locally, follow the repository's build requirements , then clone the repository , install dependencies, and start the engine: The first build compiles the Rust core and its dependencies, so give it some time. Subsequent builds reuse the build cache. Finally wrangler starts a local development server at http://127.0.0.1:8787 . Open that address to try a page in Chrome DevTools, or use it programmatically. Or you can point your AI harness at the local CDP port (agents love CDP) and watch it take full control of Kitesurf.
